story_text.value:
I made this tool because whenever I want to do a new project, there is always this awkward step of picking required tooling that has to be installed on the system. I don't want to manage it, and I don't want to keep my local env in sync with CI configuration.

There are many package managers that fill this niche already, like mise and asdf, but they have the same downside: they are a separate installation step you need to do on CI or your machine to work with the project. I wanted something small that you check in and then simply use anywhere, so I built it.

.cmd works in any shell, be it Linux, macOS, or even Windows! And it's designed to be a cross-platform tool downloader and launcher, acting as an entry point to your project's CLI tasks. TBH, I think it's crazy something like this didn't exist before...

title.value: Show HN: .cmd, cross-platform build tool manager and task launcher you check in

story_text.value:
In 2019, I was teaching science at an international school in Chiang Mai. One day before class, one of my Grade 7 students asked me about flat earth. He had heard the idea from Kyrie Irving and then spent the night on flat earth sites.

We walked through the claims and I explained why those arguments failed. He listened with interest. I was glad he'd come to me. He hadn't made up his mind yet; he was just curious. But this made me wonder if teaching the course content I was teaching was enough.

To be clear: I do think teaching facts is important. For example, when students learn about gravity, physics, and space, they're better prepared to see why flat earth arguments are wrong. The problem is we can't teach facts fast enough to combat the wide variety of misinformation and manipulation kids face on the internet every day.

This is what got me thinking that kids need to learn how to evaluate claims and information across a wide range of topics. While we can't prepare them for every false or misleading claim they might encounter, we can give them tools to assess them.

That eventually led my husband and I to build Critikid, a site for teaching kids and teens. We've been working on it for 3 years now! He does the technical work (design and coding) and I do the educational content creation.

By now, there are 5 interactive courses for ages 5-18 on logical fallacies, media literacy, emotional intelligence, statistical reasoning, and formal logic. There are also worksheets and lesson plans.

I often teach through stories, as stories make abstract critical thinking concepts concrete (and they're fun!)

If you'd like to try it, all of the courses have a free first lesson.

Are there any other topics that you think should be included in kids' critical thinking education that I've missed?

title.value: Show HN: A critical thinking site for kids and teens

story_text.value:
Zebu is a time tracking and invoicing app for freelancers and small teams. It's €5 per seat per month (billed yearly), flat, with no usage fees. There's a limited free plan for solo use.

I built it after 15 years as a solo freelancer on Harvest. After they were acquired, my renewal exploded from $12/month to ~$180/month, and unclear usage based pricing made it hard to predict how much it would always cost. The BBC even reported customers seeing increases of 1,500% - https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/clyq011414eo.

I've been working on a replacement for the past year, and am happy to say my colleagues and I now use it full-time. In many ways it even surpasses the featureset I'd had on Harvest - it's really kind of amazing what kind of custom tooling one can build these days.

I'd especially like feedback on how the migration is working from any services you might come from, any critical integrations that might be useful, and especially what might be missing for team use.

story_text.value:
I ported NHTSA's spVinDecode to TypeScript and run it on Cloudflare Workers over the official monthly vPIC dump, so decoding needs no call to NHTSA (p50 about 1.4 ms).

How it's checked:

It is compared with NHTSA's own SQL functions on the original dump in PostgreSQL. There were 0 unexplained differences on 11,000 VINs. It matches the live API on 95.4% of 1,000 VINs. The rest is newer live data.

While doing this I found that spvindecode in the PostgreSQL dump never applies VinDescriptor overrides. I wrote it up in docs/NHTSA-ERRATA.md.

Limits: only vPIC is fully live. Recalls and fuel economy are partial, and complaints/NCAP are planned. Corgi is a similar project, and I haven't benchmarked against it.

Demo: https://data.ai-kit.net/vpic

title.value: Show HN: Offline NHTSA VIN decoder, verified against NHTSA's own SQL

story_text.value:
This is my first real project; keep in mind I have no formal programming/CS background. It is hand-written; AI was only used for some conceptual questions.

Background: There's an epidemic of "fake" .flac audio files floating around: lossy audio masquerading as true lossless-quality audio. I rewrote the fakeflac.py utility in Go, adding multithreading to greatly improve performance, and increasing portability by embedding an optional WASM build of ffmpeg.

Limitations: the original fakeflac algorithm is a great starting point, but it fails to find a cutoff point with some (obviously very low quality) audio files and produces a false score of 100%. I added CLI flags to tune the cutoff detection, but future versions definitely need some work (less normalization? entirely new detection algorithm?)

title.value: Show HN: Fakeflac-go – A tool for quickly finding "fake" .flac files
